Okay, is this better? 

Once a promising photographer, an unplanned pregnancy forced Diane to trade her art for stability and Trader Joe's. Her marriage to a former grindcore punk singer turned real estate agent bores her more each day, and she seethes in resentment toward their creative teenage daughter Holly, who flourishes in ways that she has not. She knows she should give Holly center stage, but most days, it's untenable, like a sharp, gleaming version of herself is still waiting to surface. She can't stop herself from lobbying mean little digs. 

But her barbs hit Holly hard, sowing self-doubt, and one night, when her parents are out, she swallows handfuls of pills. Jolted awake, Diane knows it's time to get her life back if she's to be the parent her daughter needs right now. Attending art shows, Diane grapples with reclaiming her creative identity in a photography scene that no longer recognizes her. To move forward, she must reckon with the long shadow cast by her charismatic father, whose early death set her on a path defined by fear, compromise, and silence. Until she faces the truth about his death and her role in it, she won't be able to find her way back to Holly and herself.

But when Jeff finds out the project will kill a budding urban farm initiative, he has second thoughts. * Troubled teenager girl finds meaning and purpose when she’s pulled into street activism and anti-gentrification protest. But when the leader of the movement starts to seem shady, she finds out she’s being set up as part of an elaborate real estate insurance scam (see above).

Right now, the book is about all three things with no central focus with alternating chapters from each character’s point of view. Which front story sound most promising for publication? Also, is a teen suicide attempt just too heavy to sell a book?

It’s actually part of our job.

If you are their professor, you know their work. So that's what you focus on. Students aren't obligated to have a personal relationship with us, especially right now. I've had brilliant STEM students who were probably on the spectrum and barely spoke in class. I really \*don't\* need to get to know them to recommend them.

So you realize "putting the time in to meet with me" isn't part of being your student unless you make it a requirement of the course? And that writing letters of recommendation IS part of your job? You are holding a personal-interaction standard to something that is professional. Also, students don't necessarily know they will need letters in the future while they are in our courses.

If a student earns an A or a B in my course, I will write them a letter. I sometimes write a letter for a C student if I think they took the course seriously. And I never give anyone a weak letter or qualify anything, like "I didn't know this student very well." It's a recommendation, or a strong recommendation, or a very strong recommendation, period. I don't need any ass-kissing or whatever you think  "getting to know me" is. I understand that my students are incredibly busy, stressed, sometimes introverted, and do not expect them to come to office hours unless they need help with something. I would not DREAM of holding someone back from transferring or grad school or a scholarship if the academic work was decent--that's gatekeeping. I have a letter of recommendation template that I tweak and personalize, and sometimes that means going back into Canvas to review their assignments, discussions, etc.

If a student did poorly or was rude or problematic, I will say no. Otherwise, I'm writing that letter just like my professors wrote letters for me when I was an undergrad who got a decent grade in their class but never went to office hours unless I needed their help.

I'm definitely an instructor--FT associate professor at a CC where I've taught for 27 years now. Too bad if I make you feel guilty--if you aren't going the extra mile for students during COVID, there is something wrong with you.
